clinician.final_diagnosis: a liver abscess caused by the ingested foreign body without the sign of gastrointestinal perforation
clinician.trajectory_summary: A 66-year-old male presented with right hypochondriac pain and intermittent low-grade fever. Physical examination revealed mild tenderness in the right hypochondriac region. Initial ultrasonography showed a poorly demarcated, heterogeneous liver lesion with liquefied necrotic areas and no abdominal fluid. An abdominal CT scan further characterized the lesion and identified an abnormal high attenuation linear structure suspected to be a foreign body, with no signs of intra or extraperitoneal gas or fluid. Surgical drainage confirmed a 3 cm fishbone embedded within the liver, and no evidence of gastrointestinal perforation was found in the stomach or duodenum. Blood culture was positive for Streptococcus gordonii, while the surgical abscess drainage culture was negative. The patient was managed with fluid infusion, anthelmintics, and antibiotics, and discharged in stable condition.

key_supporting_evidence.claim: Patient presented with right hypochondriac pain and intermittent low-grade fever.
Physical examination revealed mild tenderness in the right hypochondriac region without guarding or rebound tenderness.
Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a poorly demarcated, heterogeneous lesion in liver segment BE with hypoechoic areas demonstrating a liquefied necrotic process, and no presence of abdominal fluid.
Abdominal CT scan showed a localized, peripherally enhancing, centrally hypoattenuating liver lesion (38 mm) from segment BE to segment 3.
CT scan identified an abnormal high attenuation linear structure inside the liver lesion, suspected to be a foreign body, and confirmed no intra or extraperitoneal gas or fluid.
Intraoperatively, a 3 cm fishbone was discovered embedded within the liver.
No evidence of perforation was identified in the stomach or duodenum during surgery.
Blood culture was positive for Streptococcus gordonii, and surgical abscess drainage culture was negative.
The patient was managed with fluid infusion, anthelmintics, and antibiotics, and discharged in stable condition.

ruled_out_or_less_likely_alternatives.basis: No abdominal fluid on ultrasound (E004), no intra or extraperitoneal gas or fluid on CT (E008), and no evidence of perforation in stomach or duodenum during surgery (E009).

remaining_uncertainties: Explicit historical confirmation of foreign body ingestion prior to symptom onset.

More detailed post-operative clinical course and actual hospital stay duration, as the reported 'discharged on the same day' (E006) seems to conflict with the timeline of other events (e.g., CT 2 weeks later, E008).
